articles.title: Tunisia jails opposition politician for four years over social media posts
articles.summary: Olfa ⁠Hamdi, a US-Tunisian national, was convicted of ‘plotting’ and ‘inciting’ military to disobey orders.
articles.body:
A Tunisian military court has sentenced an opposition ⁠leader to four years in prison on charges of plotting against state security and inciting the ⁠military to disobey orders, her lawyer has said.

The charges against Olfa ⁠Hamdi, a dual Tunisian and United States national, stemmed from social media posts, her lawyer Akram Moussa said on Wednesday. Hamdi has repeatedly criticised Tunisian President Kais Saied’s rule and called for a transitional government and early presidential elections.

Critics say the case against Hamdi is the latest in a crackdown on opponents of Saied.

In Tunisia’s 2024 elections, Hamdi, who was then 36, sought to run for president. Her candidacy was rejected for not meeting the 40-year age minimum for candidates.

Hamdi, the leader of the Third Republic Party, was detained at Tunisia’s main airport after disembarking from a flight in February.

She ‌had been living abroad, running a consulting firm in the US after briefly serving as the head of Tunisia’s national airline Tunisair.

Hamdi’s sentence comprises two separate two-year prison terms from two additional convictions and 80,000 dinars ($26,000) in fines, her lawyer said.

Hamdi was also sentenced in March in a separate case to two years in prison. Global human rights organisations have widely criticised the cases against her.

A US Department of State spokesperson told the AFP news agency that Washington was “closely tracking the situation”.

“The [President Donald] Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of American citizens,” he said.

Rights groups have criticised Saied, accusing him of rolling back freedoms in a 2021 power grab .

Thousands of ‌Tunisians joined the largest protest against Saied in years on Saturday, accusing him of undermining democracy and ‌mishandling ‌the economy. Opposition leaders, activists ⁠and journalists have been imprisoned during his rule.

Saied rejects accusations that he is targeting political opponents and critics, saying the law applies to everyone regardless of their position.

articles.title: Pope Leo needs no further lung cancer treatment, Vatican says
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer surgery last week was a success and no further treatment is required, the Vatican press office said in a bulletin Wednesday.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer surgery last week was a success, and no further treatment is required, the Vatican press office said in a bulletin Wednesday. “The final histological reports and molecular biology analyses of the tissue removed during the Holy Father’s surgery have been completed today,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone, the pope’s personal physician, and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, a thoracic surgery professor who led the surgical team. “The results have confirmed that the condition was a pulmonary adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized. A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the bulletin added. Pulmonary adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer, accounting for roughly 40% of all cases. It’s slow-moving and often affects nonsmokers. Leo’s announcement on October 11 that he required surgery for a “nodule” on his lung came as a shock both within and outside the Vatican, given the pope’s penchant for clean living. After a short stay at a hospital in Rome, where doctors removed the lobe of his left lung, Leo returned home on October 17. The next day, he made his first public appearance since his diagnosis, leading the Sunday Angelus from the balcony of the Apostolic Palace. “This experience has given me a profound sense of closeness to all those who are going through illness or a state of infirmity,” he told crowds of worshipers. Pope Leo’s recovery has beeen much faster than normal, according to Dr. Juanita Mora, the national medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association, who was not part of his care team. She said doctors will monitor the pope after his recent treatment, including follow-up CT scans every three to six months for the first few years, then annually to check for any regrowth. After such surgery, patients often have respiratory physiotherapy to restore breathing capacity, Mora told CNN, adding that his affected lung should regain full function. The all-clear arrives ahead of the pontiff’s planned South America trip next month. The news that the pope had cancer complicated plans for the journey, scheduled to include stops in Peru, Uruguay and Argentina and require at least 14 flights. Though the Vatican has not officially confirmed the pope’s plans for travel, Margaritora, his surgeon, told Vatican News that he saw “no clinical reasons” for canceling the trip. If the trip goes ahead, the pontiff will probably be told to walk during his travels to prevent blood clots that can form during long flights, according to Mora. The pope, she said, should get Covid-19, flu and RSV vaccines ahead of his trip for “a little extra protection in case he were to get any of the respiratory infections.” This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: Who are the terrorists? J&K and Ladakh high court questions ‘vague’ detention order
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: J&K and Ladakh HC has summoned the Srinagar deputy commissioner for a personal appearance over a “vague” preventive detention order under Public
articles.body: SRINAGAR: J&K and Ladakh HC has summoned the Srinagar deputy commissioner for a personal appearance over a “vague” preventive detention order under Public Safety Act that accused a 28-year-old man of supporting “aforementioned terrorists” without identifying a single one, prompting the court to question whether the officer had independently assessed the case or merely reproduced a police dossier.A single bench of Justice Wasim Nargal said preventive detention, which allows authorities to deprive a person of liberty without a regular criminal trial, demands the “highest degree of constitutional responsibility and procedural diligence”.“The safeguards embodied in Articles 21 and 22 of the Constitution of India are not empty formalities,” the court said, adding that the detaining authority must independently assess the material and satisfy itself that legal conditions for detention are met.The court directed the DC to appear with the detention order, police dossier, material placed before him and records showing his consideration of the case and subjective satisfaction before ordering detention under PSA.HC was hearing a habeas corpus petition filed by Zubair Amin Bangroo of Srinagar, challenging his detention under an order dated Jan 13, 2026. His counsel Nida Nazir said the allegations were vague, no FIR had been registered against him and the detention order appeared to have been passed hurriedly.The order accused Bangroo of developing close links with terrorists, supporting them logistically and morally, and allowing his home and other safe locations to be used as hideouts. However, Nazir said it neither identified the terrorists nor named the network or associates with whom Bangroo was allegedly in contact.HC found that the detention grounds referred to “aforementioned terrorists” without any preceding reference identifying a terrorist. The phrase raised a compelling question about whether the DC had independently formulated the grounds or simply reproduced the police dossier, the court said.“Personal liberty occupies a position of paramount importance in the constitutional scheme. articles.title: In 2024, a Connecticut tenant tripped over concrete outside his unlit apartment building and later lost a toe; he won a $1.6 million judgment in January 2026, but his lawyer says he has received nothing
articles.summary: A Connecticut tenant who won a $1.6 million (£1.23 million) court award after tripping over construction debris outside his unlit apartment building has
articles.body: A Connecticut tenant who won a $1.6 million (£1.23 million) court award after tripping over construction debris outside his unlit apartment building has still not received any money from his former landlord, according to his lawyer. Michael Criscuolo, 65, suffered a serious foot injury that eventually led to the amputation of one of his toes. The incident happened outside his apartment at 23 Argonne Terrace in Seymour, Connecticut, in May 2024. After his landlord failed to respond to a personal injury lawsuit, Superior Court Judge H. Gordon Hall issued a default judgment awarding Criscuolo $1.6 million in damages in January 2026. However, the landlord is now appealing the decision, delaying payment indefinitely. According to the Valley Independent Sentinel, Criscuolo's attorney, Sean Stokes of Riscassi & Davis, P.C., confirmed that the former landlord has not paid any part of the judgment. "What happened to Mr Criscuolo happens all the time. People get injured because there's a defect on a property, or they slipped on ice, that happens," Stokes told the Valley Independent Sentinel. "The difference is most of the time we have landlords and property owners that are responsible and either carry insurance coverage, or are self-insured, or show up in court when a case is filed. None of that happened here."Late-night fall leads to severe medical complicationsThe incident happened on May 24, 2024, at around 11 p.m. Criscuolo was walking from his three-story apartment building toward the property's parking lot. According to court documents cited by the Valley Independent Sentinel, the walkway and parking area had no lighting and were covered with construction materials left behind during building renovations. Criscuolo hit his foot against an exposed concrete footing hidden among the debris. The impact caused a deep wound on his foot. The wound later developed a serious infection, and doctors had to amputate one of his toes. Court records show that Criscuolo faced about $652,000 (£500,000) in medical bills for the injury and the surgeries that followed. In May 2025, Criscuolo filed a lawsuit against the property's owner, SL Seymour, LLC. He claimed that the landlord had failed to manage the property properly and keep it safe for residents.Default judgment and late legal appealsNeither SL Seymour, LLC nor its sole managing member, Sim Levenhartz, responded to the lawsuit or appeared in court. As a result, Judge Hall issued a default judgment in Criscuolo's favour. After a formal hearing to determine the amount of damages, the court awarded him $1.6 million in January 2026. Four months after the judgment was issued, a lawyer representing Levenhartz asked the court to reopen the case. Legal representative Kenneth Rozich argued on Levenhartz's behalf that the landlord had not been properly served with the original lawsuit papers. Judge Hall rejected the request to reopen the case, ruling that the legal papers had been properly delivered under Connecticut law. Levenhartz then appealed the judge's decision, leaving the case tied up in the state's higher courts. When the Valley Independent Sentinel contacted Rozich about the appeal, he declined to comment on the ongoing case.Widespread municipal fines and property issuesInvestigations by local news outlets found a wider pattern of property violations and unpaid town debts linked to the landlord and the Seymour building. According to municipal records obtained by the Valley Independent Sentinel, the nine-unit building on Argonne Terrace is now empty, with its windows boarded up. Town officials said the property has about $40,000 in unpaid municipal fines for blight, along with roughly $15,600 in unpaid property taxes. Local building inspectors had also issued a stop-work order at the property in 2025 after finding that engineering certificates submitted for the renovation work were invalid. In addition, an August report by the New Haven Independent noted that Levenhartz faces an active arrest warrant in nearby New Haven over alleged building code violations. The report also stated that he owes $259,000 in municipal blight liens linked to other residential properties he owns. Stokes said the landlord's failure to respond to court notices appears to be part of a pattern of avoiding financial responsibilities. "What we found ultimately is he appears to be doing whatever he can to avoid these types of responsibilities in the State of Connecticut," Stokes told the Valley Independent Sentinel. "The City of New Haven is having a horrible time collecting blight liens from him. My client is unfortunately part of that story." articles.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion to New Mexico after jury finds company misled consumers about data privacy
articles.summary: A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms to pay $25 billion on Wednesday after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that a political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign obtained data from ‌millions of Facebook users without their consent.
articles.body: A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms to pay $25 billion on Wednesday after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that a political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign obtained data from ‌millions of Facebook users without their consent. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said it was one of the largest, if not the largest, single state verdict against the company in American history. "Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict. Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion. A spokesperson for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The company had previously said a penalty in the billions of dollars risked violating its constitutional rights to due process and protection from excessive fines. The penalty is the largest levied against the tech giant in the wake of the Cambridge Analytica scandal. In 2019, the company was hit with a $5 billion penalty by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission stemming from the same scandal. Six other states settled their lawsuits related to Cambridge Analytica for $459.2 million as part of a $17.1 billion multistate settlement Meta reached in August to resolve states' claims that the company's platforms had harmed teen mental health. Lawsuit filed five years ago New Mexico's attorney general had sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app. The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data, how the company handles hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform and other internal policies. The company knew that third parties had broad access to users' personal data, and it tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company's bottom line, the state said. Cambridge Analytica, now defunct, worked for Trump's successful presidential campaign in 2016, and gained access to the personal information from millions of Facebook accounts for the purposes of voter profiling and targeting. It obtained that information without users' consent from a researcher who had been allowed by Facebook to deploy an app on its social media network. "It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable," Torrez told a press conference in Albuquerque after Wednesday's ruling. "I think today's judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers." Analyst Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson & Co, called the ruling costly but unlikely to impact the company's value. "Meta is worth nearly two trillion dollars, and will likely continue to appeal these cases and drag them out," Luria said. Experts expect appeal Legal experts and financial analysts said the penalty was likely to face a lengthy battle on appeal. Jurors on September 25 found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading. They said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws, based on the number of Facebook users or New Mexico residents who were the audience for each misleading statement. State law allows a penalty of up to $5,000 per violation, and directs that all of the money go to New Mexico's school system, Torrez told reporters after the verdict. At a hearing on October 1, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, had asked Mathew to award the state between $35 billion and $40 billion, saying that would be supported by the US Constitution's protections on due process and the jury's verdict. "This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price," McGinn said. In court filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45 billion, saying a higher penalty ran the risk of scaring businesses out of the state. The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer had actually been misled, the company said in court filings. Daryl Lim, an associate dean at Penn State Dickinson Law, said that while the US Constitution generally protects against excessive fines, because of the way New Mexico law is written the large size of the penalty does not automatically mean it could be overturned. Two juries sided with state The verdict was the second in six months by a Santa Fe jury in a lawsuit brought by the state of New Mexico against Meta Platforms. In the first trial, which ended in March, a Santa Fe jury ​found Meta misled users ⁠about young users’ safety on its Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp platforms and ordered the company to pay $375 million in civil penalties. After a second phase of that trial, a judge directed the company to pay $567 million into a New Mexico fund for teen mental health and ordered Meta to implement measures to protect teen Facebook and Instagram users in New Mexico.

articles.title: 7 Republicans join letter urging Trump, Musk to give Ukraine targeting access in Russia
articles.summary: A bipartisan group of nearly two dozen House members is urging President Trump to ask tech mogul Elon Musk to give Ukraine access to Starlink satellite systems to hunt for missile launchers inside Russia, according to a letter sent Wednesday and obtained exclusively by The Hill. The signatories included seven House Republicans alongside 16 Democrats,…
articles.body:
A bipartisan group of nearly two dozen House members is urging President Trump to ask tech mogul Elon Musk to give Ukraine access to Starlink satellite systems to hunt for missile launchers inside Russia, according to a letter sent Wednesday and obtained exclusively by The Hill.

The signatories included seven House Republicans alongside 16 Democrats, widening the GOP coalition looking to bring Trump back to the side of Ukraine as he has swung hard in favor of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“We are writing to urge you to ask Elon Musk to let Ukraine use the Starlink satellite internet system to hunt for missile launchers inside Russia. With one phone call, you could both save lives and give Vladimir Putin greater incentives to negotiate,” the lawmakers wrote.

“If Ukraine cannot reliably intercept Russian ‘arrows,’ it must be able to shoot the ‘archer.’ The Starlink system run by Mr. Musk’s company SpaceX could help with that.”

The Republican signatories include stalwart Ukraine supporters Reps. Joe Wilson (S.C.), Brian Fitzpatrick (Pa.) and Don Bacon (Neb.), along with Reps. Carlos Gimenez (Fla.), Jeff Hurd (Colo.), Andy Harris (Md.) and Max Miller (Ohio), who represents a heavily Ukrainian district.

“Mr. President, we all share the goal of bringing an end to the war in Ukraine and the devastating loss of life it has caused,” the lawmakers wrote in the letter sent Wednesday.

“Unfortunately, Putin presently has no intention of stopping the bloodshed.”

The letter bolsters the lobbying campaign on the Senate side led by Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), who chairs the Armed Services Committee and led a congressional delegation to Ukraine last week.

Rep. Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas) was also on that trip and penned an op-ed in The Washington Post urging the U.S. to give Ukraine expanded access to Musk’s satellites.

Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky has also pushed for more U.S. help in targeting Russia’s missile launchers.

“Mr. President, as you know, Kyiv has petitioned Mr. Musk for a carve-out to this restriction. But only you can push this matter over the goal line,” the lawmakers wrote.

Trump has called for Ukraine to stop hitting Russian oil refineries, blaming those attacks for the high diesel prices in the U.S. that are largely attributed to the war against Iran.

The bipartisan letter comes as a growing number of Republicans have expressed outrage over disruptions in Ukraine to Starlink — and its military-grade version, Starshield — that hampered air defense and offensive missions.

The Wall Street Journal reported Musk ordered a slowdown in Starlink’s services. It’s not clear how involved Trump was in the discussions surrounding the slowdown.

Some Republicans have joined Democrats in calling for an investigation into the throttling of Starlink and Starshield. Many of these same Republicans have expressed further outrage over Trump waiving sanctions on Russia to export diesel fuel, as he tries to lower prices before the midterms.

Fitzpatrick and Bacon, in particular, have threatened to disrupt Trump’s agenda after the midterms if the president does not change course on Russia and Ukraine.

This includes providing Ukraine “any and all defensive equipment,” blocking imports of Russian oil and raising sanctions against Russia, Fitzpatrick wrote on social media Monday.

“Each and every one of these items will be brought to the House Floor—and each and every one of these items will pass on the House Floor by an overwhelming margin,” he wrote.

articles.title: Penrith lab to become centre for investigating Cumbria's uplands
articles.summary: The research facility in Penrith will also help train the next generation of environmental scientists.
articles.body:
A new, purpose-built laboratory will serve as a base for scientists, universities and students to investigate Cumbria's upland landscapes, and how they respond to nature recovery.

It is hoped the research facility at RSPB Wild Haweswater, in Penrith, will become a hub for upland science, bringing researchers and conservationists together to carry out fieldwork, share expertise, and develop new collaborations.

The lab was funded by the estate of the late ornithologist Denis Summers-Smith.

"We want to build on Denis's commitment to field ecology and conservation research, creating a lasting legacy that will benefit both science and nature recovery in Cumbria and beyond," said RSPB's Will Peach.

The new lab will support current research through Cumbria Connect, whose work and scientific monitoring spans Wild Haweswater, the Lowther estate and the Lowther Valley.

Dr Mo Verhoeven, conservation scientist at Cumbria Connect, explained how the region's landscape is made up of a number of distinctive environments, including peatlands and rainforest, which play a key role in storing carbon and managing water.

"Cumbria's uplands are incredibly important for nature recovery," he said.

"We hope this laboratory will give researchers, students and conservationists a place to work together and build the evidence needed to guide restoration, both here in Cumbria and in upland landscapes further afield.

"It's about making Cumbria a much stronger base for upland science."

"Just as importantly, it will help train the next generation of environmental scientists," he said.

Cumbria Connect is part of a scheme paid for by the Arcadia Fund which was co-founded by one of the heirs to the Tetra Pak fortune.

articles.body:
Russia is going to send its first tanker with diesel to the U.S. on Thursday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said.

According to a Reuters report citing the RIA news agency and other media, Novak said Wednesday the vessel will carry 40,000 metric tons of fuel.

“Additional shipments will follow, of course. There were ​agreements reached between the two leaders. We will meet the United States’ needs, to ​the extent of our capabilities,” Novak said.

Earlier this month, President Trump said Russia would “immediately” supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and the global marketplace. In a Truth Social post on Oct. 9, the president wrote that the country would export “another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter.”

Trump’s deal with Russia prompted criticism from lawmakers across the board. In an interview with Piers Morgan, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he felt “betrayed” by Trump’s decision.

Special envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg to discuss the Russia-Ukraine war, and Putin agreed to resume trilateral talks “in principle” with Washington and Ukraine, The Associated Press reported.

During Wednesday’s talks, Putin said the country is preparing for the deliveries of Russian tankers with diesel, according to Reuters.

“They will go one after another. The ​financial component should be provided,” the Russian leader said.

Putin added that, along with diesel, Russia also would be able to supply fertilizers in “large quantities” ​to the U.S. market.

Stephen Hubbard, an American teacher who was accused of being a Ukrainian mercenary, was released Wednesday after more than four years in detention. Witkoff called the Russian leader a “humanitarian” for releasing Hubbard and faced intense backlash .

articles.title: US orders departure of embassy staff, families from Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: The State Department ordered the departure of nonemergency U.S. government employees and their family members from Saudi Arabia on Wednesday as the Iranian-backed Houthis have continued to attack the country. “As the Department has repeatedly emphasized, the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly, including beyond that immediate area,” a State Department spokesperson told The…
articles.body:
The State Department ordered the departure of nonemergency U.S. government employees and their family members from Saudi Arabia on Wednesday as the Iranian-backed Houthis have continued to attack the country.

“As the Department has repeatedly emphasized, the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly, including beyond that immediate area,” a State Department spokesperson told The Hill.

“The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority, and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them as they return to the U.S.,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

The new order comes as the Houthis are engaged in a war against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and have been attacking infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports and other critical sites that have led to civilian casualties.

Saudi Arabia’s air defense intercepted a drone targeting Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield on Wednesday, but two people were killed and another two were injured from the falling debris, the nation’s energy ministry said.

Reuters first reported on Wednesday that the U.S. government is preparing to issue an ordered departure of some personnel and family members from U.S. embassies across the Gulf. State Department spokesperson Tommy Piggot said the report is “inaccurate.”

The Agence France-Presse later reported that the U.S. ordered families of embassy staff in the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain to leave, citing a diplomatic source.

“I don’t know that they are. You are telling me something — I wouldn’t know that,” President Trump said Wednesday when asked about the reports.

The U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia put out a security alert on Wednesday about the potential for further Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia.

“U.S. citizens are reminded to follow the guidance of national alerts released by Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense via cellular broadcast,” the embassy said. “U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia require special authorization from Chief of Mission to use any airport in Saudi Arabia following recent missile and UAV attacks on airports in the Kingdom.”

articles.title: Women take to social media to break the taboo of UTIs
articles.summary: Women are sharing their experiences with chronic urinary tract infections on social media in an effort to break the stigma surrounding UTIs.
articles.body:
"The impact goes far beyond what people understand - we're talking about pain, urgency, sleepless nights and missing out on your life," Adrianne tells her roughly 8,000 followers in a video on TikTok.

For nearly five years, Adrianne has lived with a chronic urinary tract infection (UTI) - a condition it took her two years to get a diagnosis for.

In that time she was wrongly told it was colon cancer, Crohn's disease or even that her partner must have been cheating and had given her a sexually transmitted infection.

What started as one UTI in 2022 became a debilitating cycle.

"It has completely stripped me of everything: being able to work properly, my relationships, my friendships, going out, being able to have a normal social life," says Adrianne, who works in digital marketing in London.

The 29-year-old was eventually diagnosed privately with a chronic UTI - something experts estimate could affect up to 1.7 million women in the UK . Men and children are also affected.

Adrianne is not alone in sharing her story and coping mechanisms on social media to fight the stigma surrounding UTIs.

A quick search on Tiktok or Instagram shows hundreds of posts of women of all ages talking about the reality of living with recurrent and chronic UTIs.

"I felt incredibly nervous to put myself out there, but there's now this community of people who can share tips with each other, and understand each other," said Adrianne, saying her posts have had a "really positive response".

A chronic UTI, which has no official medical definition, is an infection with persistent symptoms - even after a standard course of antibiotics. It can be caused by bacteria entering the lining of your bladder.

The condition can be unpredictable, but at its worst is "completely debilitating", says Adrianne, describing "the most excruciating abdominal pain, like shooting, spasming pain."

"You need a wee all the time, but it's like weeing lava."

"It's a very claustrophobic feeling, of I'm trapped in this body that is betraying me and is in pain," she adds.

Even on a good day she struggles to leave the house as she worries about having a flare-up.

While sending a urine sample to the lab remains the gold standard to diagnose a UTI, "false negatives" can often occur, says Professor Chris Harding, a consultant urologist at Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust.

Another hurdle is the significant crossover between chronic UTIs and other conditions such as painful bladder syndrome, chronic pelvic pain and endometriosis, says Magda Kujawa, a consultant urologist at Stockport NHS Foundation Trust.

Adrianne says she felt "dismissed" by doctors while trying to get a diagnosis, and frustrated at repeatedly being given advice around hygiene and hydration, while her symptoms persisted.

Both experts say health professionals should listen to the patient's story to understand whether symptoms amount to a recurrent or chronic condition or something else entirely.

Since she started posting online, Adrianne has received messages from other young women who worry they are "dirty" and "not taking care of themselves" or that there is "something wrong with them".

"There's definitely still a lot of stigma around why people get them (UTIs), and it all just comes back to education. We're not taught about them at school," she adds.

Laura Von Müllen, 26, has also been diagnosed with a chronic UTI and documents her experience on TikTok.

She says her symptoms "really badly" impacted university, and became particularly difficult to manage when she started working. She now works remotely from Kent doing social media management.

As well as urinary symptoms, Laura says she also experiences heart palpitations and panic attacks.

"People don't understand, they think it's just a UTI and that it'll clear within three days, but I've still got mine two years later," she says.

Laura also feels there is still a lot of misconception around UTIs. "People have said to me: who have you been sleeping with then? When that's not the case."

Adrianne and Laura hope more women sharing their experience will help demystify the condition.

Harding agrees. adding that "the more we can talk about these conditions, the more people will present to appropriate specialists and get the right treatment."

But both Harding and Kujawa warn that while social media can be a useful resource, there is the risk of coming across misinformation and harmful advice, including "hacks" that could cause more harm.

"I've seen women on social media sitting in baths of disinfectant, all because they were convinced that that they were dirty, and that's why they were getting infections. And actually, that just made things ten times worse," Kujawa says.

While Adrianne and Laura's symptoms are showing improvements, they say it's a "long road to recovery".

articles.title: Trump's green card curbs test Indian tech workers' American dream
articles.summary: With immigration curbs and tech firms cutting foreign hiring, US residency is becoming a distant dream for many Indians.
articles.body:
For millions of Indians, the road to the ultimate career aspiration had a familiar script - an engineering degree to get a tech services job, then a posting in the US, repeated visa renewals and then the green card that gave them permanent residency in the country.

Earlier this month, the US announced it would suspend eight technology firms , including Microsoft, India's Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa pathway.

New and pending applications under the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, have been frozen. This is a big blow to Indians who hold a majority of H-1B visas - a temporary visa for specialists - which they used to work in the US while relying on PERM to get a green card and, ultimately, citizenship.

The latest announcement is in line with Trump's push for stricter skilled-worker immigration rules, which tech firms have been adapting to and, therefore, the impact on businesses may be minimal, experts say.

Nasscom, the trade association of India's $300bn (£226bn) technology industry, says that Indian companies have reduced the dependence on H-1B visas and are hiring more locally.

"Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited," the association adds.

Wipro said in a statement that more than 80% of its workforce in the US is locally hired. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), said its PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years. Microsoft said in a statement that it has filed for H-1B visas mostly to retain existing staff, not to import new workers.

A report in Business Standard newspaper, citing PERM Tracker, said, TCS' applications filings fell to two in 2025-26 from 513 in the previous year and 1,804 in the year before that. The report said no records were found for Infosys and Wipro for 2025-26.

BBC's email to all eight companies asking questions about the impact of the restriction and how they were supporting affected employees in the US remained unanswered.

Brokerage firm HDFC Securities said the impact on tech firms would be minimal, as PERM-linked jobs make up only a small share of revenue, even if higher-paid American workers replace them.

But the US government's decision has an impact beyond business.

A US-based senior executive with one of these eight firms told the BBC on condition of anonymity that the new PERM restriction will "not break the business", but the impact is more "intense" at a human level.

"A good number of people we know are stuck in a space where they have spent some years in the US but their green card application hasn't moved. Even if they are ready to move back to India, their children don't want to because they grew up here," he said.

Recent policy moves have deepened uncertainty and amplified online hostility towards Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders.

Researchers at Stop AAPI Hate, a US non-profit that combats anti-Asian and Pacific Islander discrimination, have reported a sharp increase in anti-South Asian online sentiment since the 2024 US election, with Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders being frequent targets.

While barring the eight tech companies from PERM, US Vice President JD Vance too referred to foreign professionals holding H-1B visas as "foreign indentured servants".

While he later acknowledged that it was an "imperfect" rhetoric, his remark drew sharp criticism from India's foreign ministry which called it "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive" for the colonial connotation.

Poorvi Chothani, founder and managing partner of global immigration law firm LawQuest, said many came to the US for better prospects, borrowing heavily to study and build careers. But as rules tighten now, they have fewer options and less ability to absorb the costs.

Immigration experts believe that as pathways for residency become limited, some may reconsider their future in the US, while others may choose not to move at all.

Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Immigration Policy Lab, told BBC that despite alternate ways to get residency, not many may be feasible.

While moving to another firm not covered by the suspension is an option, he flags that it's unclear if those firms would be open to hiring immigrants given "the fear of retaliation".

Besides, it's also a tough time to change jobs.

The technology industry has already been reshaped by layoffs, cost-cutting and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), making career moves tougher.

But there are other routes to a US green card. People with exceptional accomplishments or whose work advances national interests may be eligible for categories that bypass the PERM labour certification process.

Applicants can also qualify for permanent residency by investing at least $800,000 in eligible US enterprises.

Gulek warns some of these categories "may be targeted next."

While Chothani says some are so keen to stay in the US that they are considering the EB-5 investor route but may not have enough capital to invest.

Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025, representing 79% of the total pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP).

Their report projects wait times ranging from five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing labour certification or employment-based immigration petitions from January 2026, depending on the visa category.

Like other recent immigration measures, the PERM suspension may face federal court challenges. But together, these moves signal a more restrictive climate for those hoping to study, work or settle in the US.

Earlier, the Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B visa petitions, a measure that was later struck down by federal courts. More recently, it has also proposed a $70,000 fee for universities recommending international students for a programme that allows graduates to work in the country after completing their studies.

"This trend is not changing anytime soon," said an Indian professional, who spoke to BBC on condition of anonymity and has transitioned to an H-1B visa recently after a "long wait". He says both the Republican Party and the Democratic Party agree immigration laws need reform, even if they disagree on how.

Some research suggests that restrictions could shift jobs to India rather than to American workers. This is supported by industry players saying that they are already witnessing an increase in companies offshoring work.

"Companies benefit from cost arbitrage when they move work offshore. Post Covid, there is also greater acceptance and appreciation for remote work from clients," the executive from the tech firm earlier quoted says.

Experts believe America's appetite for Indian tech talent is unlikely to disappear. What may be changing is how it taps that talent. For Indian professionals, that could mean rewriting the script about building a future in the US.
